recent_posts.title: I Built a Tool to Manage Multiple AI Agents at Once
MCP vs CLI for AI agents connecting to remote servers
recent_posts.summary: MCP (Model Context Protocol) injects every connected tool's name, description, and parameter schema into the LLM's context window on every turn, burning thousands of tokens before a single question is asked. As an alternative, CLIs can serve as the communication channel between agents and remote servers — for well-known tools like kubectl, gh, or AWS CLI, the LLM already knows how to use them with zero context cost. For custom or internal CLIs, lightweight 'skill files' (a few lines describing the tool) can teach the LLM what it needs, at a fraction of the token cost of MCP definitions. The trade-off: MCP offers centralized maintenance and standardized discovery across agent platforms, while CLIs require per-machine installation and distributed maintenance. The verdict: use CLIs for well-known tools, lean MCP for custom internal tools with few well-designed endpoints, and CLI with skill files when context footprint matters most. Both can coexist since the same backend API can expose MCP, HTTP, and CLI interfaces simultaneously.

recent_posts.title: Why 65% of software costs are in maintenance and what AI will do about it
recent_posts.summary: Senior developers spend less than a third of their time writing code, yet AI tools currently optimize only that minority. The real opportunity lies in the 65% of software costs that occur post-deployment in maintenance. As AI agents improve at understanding codebases, handling integrations, and managing deployments, the traditional build-versus-buy calculus will fundamentally shift.

recent_posts.title: Why AI threatens software vendors more than software engineers
recent_posts.summary: AI is reshaping the software industry not by replacing engineers directly, but by enabling companies that use software to build their own tools instead of buying them. Software vendors are losing market cap and laying off workers as the build-vs-buy math shifts. Meanwhile, engineers at non-tech companies like banks, retailers, and manufacturers may see increased demand. Key data points include AT&T building a 6-week project in 20 minutes with AI, 39% of companies already replacing SaaS tools with custom builds, and over $1 trillion erased from software market cap in February 2026. The core argument: the real threat to software vendor jobs isn't AI writing code — it's AI helping their customers write code instead of paying for SaaS.

recent_posts.title: AI job risk for software engineers depends on where you work
recent_posts.summary: Software engineers at product companies (those that sell software) face real AI-driven job risk, while engineers at non-tech companies like banks, retailers, and manufacturers may actually see increased job security. The reasoning: non-tech companies are poised to build significantly more software than before, driven by AI capabilities, making in-house engineers more valuable rather than less.

recent_posts.title: AI Bolted Onto Old Systems = The New Lift-and-Shift
recent_posts.summary: Drawing a parallel to the early Kubernetes 'lift-and-shift' mistake, this piece argues that bolting AI onto legacy systems without rethinking architecture or culture yields little to no benefit. Just as containerizing old apps without redesigning them failed to deliver Kubernetes' promised gains, treating AI as an add-on rather than a core part of how work gets done leads to disappointment.

recent_posts.title: How cheap experimentation changes the way we build products
recent_posts.summary: AI and modern tooling have dramatically lowered the cost of being wrong when building software. Instead of carefully planning months-long bets, developers and builders can now run rapid, cheap experiments — shipping quickly, testing with real users, discarding failures, and iterating until something works. The competitive advantage shifts from having the best first idea to being able to try the most ideas in the shortest time.

recent_posts.title: Why denying AI benefits is as risky as ignoring its problems
recent_posts.summary: Adopting AI is no longer optional for developers and companies. The key differentiator is not whether to adopt AI, but how well and how continuously you invest in it as the landscape evolves. Those doing it right are thriving; those ignoring it or doing it poorly are falling behind. Dismissing AI's benefits is now as risky as ignoring its problems.

recent_posts.title: Most AI Agent Failures Are Context Failures
recent_posts.summary: AI agents produce poor results not because of model limitations, but because developers fail to provide sufficient context. Teams getting great results feed agents architecture docs, coding conventions, security requirements, and runbooks — everything needed to understand the specific codebase. The key differentiator is context quality, not model choice.

recent_posts.title: Stopping junior developer hiring threatens the future of tech leadership
recent_posts.summary: The tech industry's trend of not hiring junior developers is creating a long-term talent pipeline crisis. Without entry-level engineers gaining experience today, there will be a severe shortage of qualified senior engineers and technical leaders in 5 to 10 years. The industry is effectively undermining its own future by cutting off the path through which expertise is developed.

Self-hosting LLMs costs 10 to 30 times more than using APIs
top_posts.summary: A cost analysis arguing against self-hosting large language models. Running frontier open-weight models like Kimi K2.5 requires 4-16 Nvidia H100 GPUs, costing $8,000-$35,000/month in cloud rentals or $150,000-$300,000+ in the first year for owned hardware. By contrast, API access to the same models costs $300-$800/month — 10 to 30 times cheaper. Even smaller models on consumer hardware take years to recoup API savings. The piece also warns that 'open weight' is not 'open source': licenses like Llama's have real restrictions and can change at any time. The recommendation is to use cheap vendor APIs while AI companies are subsidizing costs with VC and government money, avoid lock-in by staying provider-agnostic, and only consider self-hosting in special cases like air-gapped environments or massive existing GPU infrastructure.

top_posts.title: How AI shifted the software development bottleneck from writing to verifying code
top_posts.summary: As AI makes code generation fast and cheap, the real bottleneck in software development has shifted. The scarce resources are now what surrounds the code: upfront architecture and context-setting before generation, and critical verification, review, and judgment afterward. Developers must now excel at determining whether AI-generated code is correct, fits the system, and will hold up in production.
